claim: Energy dissipation through interscapular brown adipose tissue (iBAT) thermogenesis is an important contributor to adaptive energy expenditure.
source: Energy dissipation through interscapular brown adipose tissue (iBAT) thermogenesis is an important contributor to adaptive energy expenditure.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract that represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: Internal energy surfeit promotes recruitment of interscapular brown adipose tissue (iBAT) thermogenesis, increasing energy expenditure and therefore limiting weight gain.
source: Internal energy surfeit, typically achieved via maintenance on energy dense food in a laboratory setting, promotes recruitment of interscapular brown adipose tissue (iBAT) thermogenesis, increasing energy expenditure and therefore limiting weight gain (Bachman et al., 2002; Feldmann et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bachman et al., 2002 and Feldmann et al., 2009.

claim: Energy expenditure is robustly decreased in energy-restricted rodents and humans.
source: Conversely, energy expenditure is robustly decreased in energy-restricted rodents and humans (Ravussin et al., 2012; Leibel et al., 1995).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ravussin et al., 2012 and Leibel et al., 1995.

claim: Sympathetic nervous outflow to iBAT modulates adaptive energy expenditure by promoting iBAT thermogenesis.
source: Sympathetic nervous outflow to iBAT modulates adaptive energy expenditure by promoting iBAT thermogenesis (Bartness et al., 2010) and is modulated by internal energy availability (Brito et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bartness et al., 2010 and Brito et al., 2008.

claim: Sympathetic nervous outflow to iBAT is modulated by internal energy availability.
source: Sympathetic nervous outflow to iBAT modulates adaptive energy expenditure by promoting iBAT thermogenesis (Bartness et al., 2010) and is modulated by internal energy availability (Brito et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Brito et al., 2008.

claim: Melanocortinergic circuits have been implicated in the control of sympathetic outflow to iBAT.
source: Melanocortinergic circuits, one of the best characterized central energy-sensing network regulating energy balance, have been implicated in the control of sympathetic outflow to iBAT (Bartness et al., 2010; Small et al., 2003)
evidence: Supported by citations to Bartness et al., 2010 and Small et al., 2003.

claim: Orexigenic neurons expressing agouti-related peptide (AGRP) and neuropeptide Y (NPY) form a discrete population of about 10,000 cells residing in the arcuate nucleus of the mouse hypothalamus (ARH).
source: Orexigenic neurons expressing agouti-related peptide (AGRP) and neuropeptide Y (NPY) form a discrete population of about 10,000 cells residing in the arcuate nucleus of the mouse hypothalamus (ARH).
evidence: This is a statement of established anatomical knowledge.

claim: AGRP neurons respond to bidirectional changes in energy availability, are activated by fasting, low glucose levels and ghrelin, and are inhibited by leptin, insulin, refeeding and high glucose levels.
source: These neurons respond to bidirectional changes in energy availability, are activated by fasting, low glucose levels and ghrelin, and are inhibited by leptin, insulin, refeeding and high glucose levels (Chen et al., 2015; Könner et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chen et al., 2015 and Könner et al., 2007.

claim: Aphagia is observed in mice with specific ablation of AGRP neurons during adulthood.
source: Their essential role in the bidirectional control of energy intake can be appreciated by the aphagia observed in mice with specific ablation of this neuronal population during adulthood (Luquet et al., 2005; Gropp et al., 2005)
evidence: Supported by citations to Luquet et al., 2005 and Gropp et al., 2005.

claim: Opto- or chemogenetic activation of AGRP neurons produces a voracious feeding response in sated mice.
source: and the voracious feeding response upon opto- or chemogenetic activation of AGRP neurons in sated mice (Aponte et al., 2011; Krashes et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Aponte et al., 2011 and Krashes et al., 2011.

claim: AGRP neurons regulate energy expenditure.
source: Initial evidence indicates that AGRP neurons also regulate energy expenditure (Krashes et al., 2011)
evidence: Supported by citation to Krashes et al., 2011.

claim: Chemogenetic activation of AGRP neurons rapidly suppresses iBAT temperature in food-deprived mice without access to food.
source: As expected, activation of AGRP neurons rapidly suppressed iBAT temperature (Figure 1a)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1a.

claim: Chemogenetic activation of AGRP neurons rapidly suppresses energy expenditure in food-deprived mice without access to food.
source: activation of AGRP neurons rapidly suppressed iBAT temperature (Figure 1a) and energy expenditure (Figure 1b) despite increasing locomotor activity (Figure 1c) when mice were maintained in a food-free environment following CNO administration.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: Chemogenetic activation of AGRP neurons increases locomotor activity in food-deprived mice without access to food.
source: activation of AGRP neurons rapidly suppressed iBAT temperature (Figure 1a) and energy expenditure (Figure 1b) despite increasing locomotor activity (Figure 1c) when mice were maintained in a food-free environment following CNO administration.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: Local administration of ghrelin into the mediobasal hypothalamus (MBH) of wild-type mice decreased iBAT temperature.
source: Local administration of ghrelin, an endogenous activator of AGRP neurons, into the mediobasal hypothalamus (MBH) of wild-type mice decreased iBAT temperature (Figure 1—figure supplement 1c)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1c.

claim: iBAT norepinephrine turnover (NETO) was significantly lower in CNO-treated mice compared to vehicle-treated mice.
source: In CNO-treated mice, iBAT NETO was significantly lower than in vehicle-treated mice (Figure 1d)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1d.

claim: AGRP activation rapidly suppresses sympathetic output to iBAT.
source: In CNO-treated mice, iBAT NETO was significantly lower than in vehicle-treated mice (Figure 1d), supporting the conclusion that AGRP activation rapidly suppresses sympathetic output to iBAT.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from NETO data in Figure 1d.

claim: Circulating thyroxine (T4) levels remained unchanged during the first 45 min following CNO administration in AGRP-activated mice.
source: In contrast, circulating thyroxine (T4) and FGF-21 levels remained unchanged during the first 45 min following CNO administration (Figure 1—figure supplement 1d and e)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1d.

claim: Circulating FGF-21 levels remained unchanged during the first 45 min following CNO administration in AGRP-activated mice.
source: In contrast, circulating thyroxine (T4) and FGF-21 levels remained unchanged during the first 45 min following CNO administration (Figure 1—figure supplement 1d and e)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1e.

claim: iBAT expression of thermogenic genes did not change within an acute 1 hr time-frame following CNO administration in AGRP-activated mice.
source: Consistent with previous reports (Ruan et al., 2014), we did not observe any changes in iBAT expression of thermogenic genes within an acute 1 hr time-frame following CNO administration (Figure 1—figure supplement 1f).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1f and citation to Ruan et al., 2014.

claim: iBAT recruitment is not involved in the rapid decrease in iBAT temperature observed as soon as 1 hr after AGRP neuronal activation.
source: These results indicate that iBAT recruitment is not involved in the rapid decrease in iBAT temperature observed as soon as 1 hr after AGRP neuronal activation.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the lack of change in thermogenic gene expression.

claim: Inhibitory phosphorylation of HSL on Ser565 was significantly increased in the iBAT of CNO-treated mice 1 hr after CNO administration.
source: In contrast, inhibitory phosphorylation of HSL on Ser565 was significantly increased in the iBAT of CNO-treated mice (Figure 1e).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1e.

claim: AMPK activatory phosphorylation was robustly increased in the iBAT of CNO-treated mice 1 hr after CNO administration.
source: Accordingly, we observed a robust increase in AMPK activatory phosphorylation in the iBAT of CNO-treated mice (Figure 1e).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1e.

claim: At baseline and in vehicle-treated animals, iBAT temperature was consistently 1°C higher than core temperature.
source: At baseline and in vehicle-treated animals, iBAT temperature was consistently 1°C higher than core temperature (Figure 1—figure supplement 1h).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1h.

claim: Upon CNO administration, iBAT temperature fell rapidly and reached core temperature within 15 min in AGRP-activated mice.
source: Upon CNO administration, iBAT temperature fall rapidly and reached core temperature within 15 min
evidence: Supported by experimental observation.

claim: Suppression of iBAT thermogenesis following AGRP activation is driving iBAT and core temperature responses.
source: Upon CNO administration, iBAT temperature fall rapidly and reached core temperature within 15 min, indicating that suppression of iBAT thermogenesis under these conditions is driving iBAT and core temperature responses.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the observation that iBAT temperature reaches core temperature.

claim: At thermoneutral zone (30°C), the effects of AGRP activation on iBAT temperature, energy expenditure and locomotor activity were attenuated but remained statistically significant.
source: Under these conditions, the effects of AGRP activation on iBAT temperature, energy expenditure and locomotor activity were attenuated, but remained statistically significant (Figure 1f–h).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1f-h.

claim: The AGRP-iBAT circuit can be engaged independently of thermoregulation.
source: This result further directly implicates iBAT thermogenic activity in the response to AGRP activation and indicates that the AGRP-iBAT circuit can be engaged independently of thermoregulation.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experiments at thermoneutrality.

claim: At 4°C, AGRP neuronal activation reduced iBAT temperature to a similar extent as at ambient temperature.
source: At 4°C, a condition under which thermoregulatory iBAT thermogenesis is strongly activated (Brito et al., 2008), AGRP neuronal activation reduced iBAT temperature to a similar extent as at ambient temperature (Figure 1—figure supplement 1i)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1i and citation to Brito et al., 2008.

claim: The dynamic range of AGRP-iBAT circuit function is dissociable from environmental temperature and cold-induced thermoregulation.
source: At 4°C, a condition under which thermoregulatory iBAT thermogenesis is strongly activated (Brito et al., 2008), AGRP neuronal activation reduced iBAT temperature to a similar extent as at ambient temperature (Figure 1—figure supplement 1i), reinforcing the idea that the dynamic range of AGRP-iBAT circuit function is dissociable from environmental temperature and cold-induced thermoregulation.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experiments at 4°C.

claim: Activation of AGRP neurons increases locomotor activity and produces a substantial sustained decrease in energy expenditure through a suppression of iBAT thermogenic activity.
source: Thus, activation of AGRP neurons increases locomotor activity and produces a substantial sustained decrease in energy expenditure through a suppression of iBAT thermogenic activity.
evidence: Summary conclusion drawn from multiple experimental observations.

claim: Activation of AGRP neurons in mice with access to food increased locomotor activity and energy intake but failed to alter iBAT temperature and energy expenditure.
source: Under these conditions, activation of AGRP neurons increased locomotor activity and energy intake but failed to alter iBAT temperature and energy expenditure (Figure 2a–c)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2a-c.

claim: Energy availability modulates the AGRP-iBAT circuit.
source: Under these conditions, activation of AGRP neurons increased locomotor activity and energy intake but failed to alter iBAT temperature and energy expenditure (Figure 2a–c), indicating that energy availability modulates the AGRP-iBAT circuit.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experiments with food access.

claim: In refed mice placed in food-free cages after CNO injection, AGRP neuronal activation suppressed iBAT temperature and energy expenditure.
source: In that context, AGRP neuronal activation suppressed iBAT temperature and energy expenditure (Figure 2d–2f)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2d-f.

claim: Internal signals of energy availability are not sufficient to blunt the AGRP-iBAT hypometabolic response.
source: In that context, AGRP neuronal activation suppressed iBAT temperature and energy expenditure (Figure 2d–2f), suggesting that internal signals of energy availability are not sufficient to blunt the AGRP-iBAT hypometabolic response.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experiments in refed mice.

claim: iBAT temperature and energy expenditure were rapidly restored in CNO-treated mice upon food reintroduction.
source: We noticed that iBAT temperature and energy expenditure were rapidly restored in CNO-treated mice upon food reintroduction in design 1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a and b)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1a and b.

claim: The presence of food rapidly resets the AGRP-iBAT circuit.
source: We noticed that iBAT temperature and energy expenditure were rapidly restored in CNO-treated mice upon food reintroduction in design 1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a and b), suggesting that the presence of food rapidly resets the AGRP-iBAT circuit.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from food reintroduction experiments.

claim: Presenting caged-food to CNO-treated mice rapidly increased iBAT temperature to levels similar to those measured in controls.
source: Presenting caged-food to CNO-treated mice rapidly increased iBAT temperature (Figure 2g) and energy expenditure (Figure 2h) to levels similar to those measured in controls
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2g.

claim: Presenting caged-food to CNO-treated mice rapidly increased energy expenditure to levels similar to those measured in controls.
source: Presenting caged-food to CNO-treated mice rapidly increased iBAT temperature (Figure 2g) and energy expenditure (Figure 2h) to levels similar to those measured in controls
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2h.

claim: The effect of caged-food presentation on iBAT temperature and energy expenditure was transient and lasted for about 1 hr.
source: Presenting caged-food to CNO-treated mice rapidly increased iBAT temperature (Figure 2g) and energy expenditure (Figure 2h) to levels similar to those measured in controls, an effect that was transient and lasted for about 1 hr.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2g and 2h.

claim: Presentation of an inedible empty container to naïve animals failed to alter iBAT temperature and energy expenditure.
source: Importantly, presentation of an inedible empty container to naïve animals failed to alter iBAT temperature and energy expenditure (Figure 2—figure supplement 1c–d)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1c-d.

claim: The stress response to the introduction of an object to naïve mice is not sufficient to produce the restoration in iBAT temperature seen with presentation of food sensory cues.
source: Importantly, presentation of an inedible empty container to naïve animals failed to alter iBAT temperature and energy expenditure (Figure 2—figure supplement 1c–d), indicating that the stress response to the introduction of an object to naïve mice is not sufficient to produce the restoration in iBAT temperature seen with presentation of food sensory cues.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from empty container control experiment.

claim: Pre-ingestive food detection is sufficient to apprehensively turn off the AGRP-iBAT circuit suppressing iBAT thermogenesis and energy expenditure.
source: These results indicate that pre-ingestive food detection is sufficient to apprehensively turn off the AGRP-iBAT circuit suppressing iBAT thermogenesis and energy expenditure.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from caged-food experiments.

claim: The AGRP-iBAT circuit integrates sensory and endogenous signals of energy availability in the regulation of iBAT thermogenic activity and energy expenditure to promote energy sparing when fuel availability is scarce.
source: Thus, the AGRP-iBAT circuit integrates sensory and endogenous signals of energy availability in the regulation of iBAT thermogenic activity and energy expenditure to promote energy sparing when fuel availability is scarce.
evidence: Summary conclusion drawn from multiple experimental observations.

claim: Refeeding for 1 hr following an overnight fast significantly increased p-mTOR expression in ARH NPY neurons.
source: Refeeding for 1 hr following an overnight fast significantly increased p-mTOR expression in ARH NPY neurons (Figure 3a and d).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3a and d.

claim: p-mTOR activation following refeeding occurs only in 15% of ARH NPY/AGRP neurons.
source: Importantly, p-mTOR activation following refeeding occurs only in 15% of ARH NPY/AGRP neurons
evidence: Supported by quantification of immunofluorescence data.

claim: Postprandial changes in energy availability is coupled to changes in mTOR signaling only in a subpopulation of ARH NPY/AGRP neurons.
source: Importantly, p-mTOR activation following refeeding occurs only in 15% of ARH NPY/AGRP neurons, supporting the conclusion that postprandial changes in energy availability is coupled to changes in mTOR signaling only in a subpopulation of ARH NPY/AGRP neurons.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the observation that only 15% of neurons show p-mTOR activation.

claim: Costained neurons (p-mTOR+ NPY/AGRP neurons) were mostly absent from the rostral ARH and concentrated in the ventro-medial neurons of the caudal ARH.
source: Costained neurons were mostly absent from the rostral ARH (−1.22 to −1.6 mm post Bregma [Paxinos and Franklin, 2001]) and concentrated in the ventro-medial neurons of the caudal ARH (−1.7 mm to −2 mm post bregma [Paxinos and Franklin, 2001]) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1d and citation to Paxinos and Franklin, 2001.

claim: After 2 days of HF feeding, iBAT thermogenesis was increased.
source: We confirmed that after 2 days of HF feeding, iBAT thermogenesis was increased (Figure 3—figure supplement 1e and f)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1e and f.

claim: After 2 days of HF feeding, energy expenditure was increased.
source: We confirmed that after 2 days of HF feeding, iBAT thermogenesis was increased (Figure 3—figure supplement 1e and f) leading to an increase in energy expenditure (Figure 3—figure supplement 1g), as previously reported (Liu et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1g and citation to Liu et al., 2014.

claim: mTOR signaling was upregulated in NPY/AGRP neurons after 2 days of HF feeding, only in a small group of this neuronal population.
source: We observed that mTOR signaling was also upregulated in NPY/AGRP neurons in this context, again only in a small group of this neuronal population (Figure 3b and e).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3b and e.

claim: In nutritional conditions under which iBAT thermogenic activity is engaged, mTOR activity is increased in a subpopulation of AGRP/NPY neurons in which metabolic signals are coupled to changes in mTOR signaling.
source: These data indicate that in nutritional conditions under which iBAT thermogenic activity is engaged, mTOR activity is increased in a subpopulation of AGRP/NPY neurons in which metabolic signals are coupled to changes in mTOR signaling.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from refeeding and HF feeding experiments.

claim: mTOR in AGRP neurons may mediate changes in sympathetic tone to iBAT during refeeding and HF feeding.
source: These findings raise the possibility that mTOR in AGRP neurons mediate changes in sympathetic tone to iBAT under these conditions.
evidence: Speculative statement based on observed correlations.

claim: In control mice exposed to an empty container, p-mTOR was absent from ARH NPY-GFP neurons.
source: In control mice exposed to an empty container, p-mTOR was absent from ARH NPY-GFP neurons (Figure 3c and f).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3c and f.

claim: 30% ARH NPY-GFP neurons expressed p-mTOR in response to 30 min exposure to caged food.
source: In contrast, 30% ARH NPY-GFP neurons expressed p-mTOR in response to 30 min exposure to caged food.
evidence: Supported by quantification of immunofluorescence data.

claim: mTOR signaling in AGRP neurons, in addition to responding to acute (refeeding) and chronic (48 hr HF feeding) internal signals of energy availability, also responds to environmental food-related cues.
source: These data indicate that mTOR signaling in AGRP neurons, in addition to responding to acute (refeeding) and chronic (48 hr HF feeding) internal signals of energy availability, also responds to environmental food-related cues.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from caged food experiments.

claim: Rapamycin increased the expression of c-fos in Npy-GFP neurons in refed mice.
source: Rapamycin increased the expression of cfos in Npy -GFP neurons (Figure 3g and h)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3g and h.

claim: mTORC1 signaling negatively regulates the activity of AGRP/NPY neurons.
source: Rapamycin increased the expression of cfos in Npy -GFP neurons (Figure 3g and h), supporting the interpretation that mTORC1 signaling negatively regulates the activity of AGRP/NPY neurons.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from rapamycin-induced c-fos expression.

claim: Rapamycin-mediated inhibition of MBH mTORC1 in refed mice significantly reduced iBAT temperature.
source: Rapamycin-mediated inhibition of MBH mTORC1 in refed mice significantly reduced iBAT temperature (Figure 3i)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3i.

claim: Rapamycin-mediated inhibition of MBH mTORC1 in refed mice significantly reduced energy expenditure.
source: Rapamycin-mediated inhibition of MBH mTORC1 in refed mice significantly reduced iBAT temperature (Figure 3i), energy expenditure (Figure 3j)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3j.

claim: Rapamycin-mediated inhibition of MBH mTORC1 in refed mice altered iBAT thermogenic gene expression.
source: Rapamycin-mediated inhibition of MBH mTORC1 in refed mice significantly reduced iBAT temperature (Figure 3i), energy expenditure (Figure 3j), and altered iBAT thermogenic gene expression (Figure 3k)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3k.

claim: Rapamycin-mediated inhibition of MBH mTORC1 in refed mice did not significantly affect locomotor activity.
source: Rapamycin-mediated inhibition of MBH mTORC1 in refed mice significantly reduced iBAT temperature (Figure 3i), energy expenditure (Figure 3j), and altered iBAT thermogenic gene expression (Figure 3k) without significantly affecting locomotor activity (Figure 3—figure supplement 1h).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1h.

claim: Activation of MBH mTORC1 using the amino acid L-leucine produced an increase in iBAT temperature in fasted mice.
source: Conversely, activation of MBH mTORC1 using the amino acid L-leucine produced an increase in iBAT temperature in fasted mice (Figure 3l)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3l.

claim: Activation of MBH mTORC1 using L-leucine did not produce changes in energy expenditure in fasted mice.
source: Conversely, activation of MBH mTORC1 using the amino acid L-leucine produced an increase in iBAT temperature in fasted mice (Figure 3l) but did not produce changes in energy expenditure (Figure 3—figure supplement 1i).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1i.

claim: Acute changes in MBH mTORC1 signaling are associated with bidirectional changes in iBAT thermogenesis.
source: Thus, acute changes in MBH mTORC1 signaling are associated with bidirectional changes in iBAT thermogenesis.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from rapamycin and leucine experiments.

claim: Over 95% of the cells expressing the pCDH-CMV-FLEX-HA-S6K1-F5a construct were Npy-GFP neurons.
source: Ha staining indicated that over 95% of the cells expressing the construct were Npy-GFP neurons and that over 60% of Npy-GFP cells expressed the construct (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1a.

claim: Over 60% of Npy-GFP cells expressed the pCDH-CMV-FLEX-HA-S6K1-F5a construct.
source: Ha staining indicated that over 95% of the cells expressing the construct were Npy-GFP neurons and that over 60% of Npy-GFP cells expressed the construct (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1a.

claim: Increased expression of p-rpS6 in ARH Npy-GFP neurons confirmed constitutive activation of the pathway in AGRP neurons of Agrp-CA-S6 mice compared to controls.
source: Increased expression of the active form of ribosomal protein S6 (phosphorylated at Ser 240–244, p-rpS6, main downstream effector of S6K) in ARH Npy-GFP neurons confirmed constitutive activation of the pathway in AGRP neurons of Agrp-CA-S6 mice compared to controls (Figure 4—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Constitutive activation of S6K1 in AGRP neurons had no effect on food intake when mice were maintained on a chow diet.
source: Constitutive activation of S6K1 in AGRP neurons had no effect on food intake (Figure 4a)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: Constitutive activation of S6K1 in AGRP neurons had no effect on body weight gain when mice were maintained on a chow diet.
source: Constitutive activation of S6K1 in AGRP neurons had no effect on food intake (Figure 4a), body weight gain (Figure 4—figure supplement 1c)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1c.

claim: Constitutive activation of S6K1 in AGRP neurons had no effect on adiposity when mice were maintained on a chow diet.
source: Constitutive activation of S6K1 in AGRP neurons had no effect on food intake (Figure 4a), body weight gain (Figure 4—figure supplement 1c), adiposity (Figure 4—figure supplement 1d)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1d.

claim: Constitutive activation of S6K1 in AGRP neurons had no effect on glucose tolerance when mice were maintained on a chow diet.
source: Constitutive activation of S6K1 in AGRP neurons had no effect on food intake (Figure 4a), body weight gain (Figure 4—figure supplement 1c), adiposity (Figure 4—figure supplement 1d) or glucose tolerance (Figure 4—figure supplement 1e) when mice were maintained on a chow diet.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1e.

claim: Manipulation of mTORC1 signaling in AGRP neurons does not produce loss of AGRP function.
source: Given the crucial role of AGRP neurons in feeding behavior and survival (Luquet et al., 2005), these results indicate that manipulation of mTORC1 signaling in AGRP neurons does not produce loss of AGRP function.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the lack of effect on food intake and body weight, with citation to Luquet et al., 2005.

claim: Agrp-CA-S6 mice were protected against body weight gain upon exposure to a HF diet.
source: Upon exposure to a HF diet, Agrp-CA-S6 mice were protected against body weight gain (Figure 4b).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: Constitutive activation of S6K1 in AGRP neurons did not affect energy intake during the transition from chow to HF diet.
source: Constitutive activation of S6K1 in AGRP neurons did not affect energy intake (Figure 4a)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: Constitutive activation of S6K1 in AGRP neurons produced a significant increase in night-time energy expenditure under HF diet.
source: Constitutive activation of S6K1 in AGRP neurons did not affect energy intake (Figure 4a) but produced a significant increase in night-time energy expenditure under HF diet (Figure 4c).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4c.

claim: Chronic changes in S6K1 signaling in AGRP neurons do not produce an overall change in AGRP activity, but rather modulate the activity of a specific subpopulation of AGRP neurons regulating energy expenditure.
source: The specific implication of energy expenditure in this metabolic phenotype, and the preservation of feeding behavior, support the conclusion that chronic changes in S6K1 signaling in AGRP neurons do not produce an overall change in AGRP activity, but rather modulate the activity of a specific subpopulation of AGRP neurons regulating energy expenditure.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the dissociation between energy expenditure and feeding effects.

claim: Substrate utilization was similar between Agrp-CA-S6 and control groups on chow.
source: Substrate utilization was similar between groups on chow but fat utilization was substantially increased after the switch to the HF diet in Agrp-CA-S6 mice (Figure 4d).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4d.

claim: Fat utilization was substantially increased after the switch to the HF diet in Agrp-CA-S6 mice.
source: Substrate utilization was similar between groups on chow but fat utilization was substantially increased after the switch to the HF diet in Agrp-CA-S6 mice (Figure 4d).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4d.

claim: Locomotor activity significantly increased in Agrp-CA-S6 mice after the transition to the HF diet.
source: Likewise, locomotor activity significantly increased in Agrp-CA-S6 mice after the transition to the HF diet (Figure 4e).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4e.

claim: Night-time iBAT temperature was significantly increased in Agrp-CA-S6 mice.
source: Night-time iBAT temperature was significantly increased in Agrp-CA-S6 mice (Figure 4f)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4f.

claim: mRNA expression of iBAT thermogenic markers was increased in Agrp-CA-S6 mice.
source: Night-time iBAT temperature was significantly increased in Agrp-CA-S6 mice (Figure 4f) and consistently, mRNA expression of iBAT thermogenic markers was increased (Figure 4g)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4g.

claim: Increased iBAT activation contributes to the elevated energy expenditure and reduced weight gain observed in Agrp-CA-S6 mice.
source: Night-time iBAT temperature was significantly increased in Agrp-CA-S6 mice (Figure 4f) and consistently, mRNA expression of iBAT thermogenic markers was increased (Figure 4g), suggesting a role for increased iBAT activation in the elevated energy expenditure and reduced weight gain observed in these mice.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from iBAT temperature and gene expression data.

claim: The amplitude of iBAT thermogenic response to β-adrenergic stimulation was similar between Agrp-CA-S6 and control groups.
source: The amplitude of iBAT thermogenic response to β-adrenergic stimulation was similar between groups (Figure 4h).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4h.

claim: Elevated iBAT thermogenesis in Agrp-CA-S6 mice was not the result of an impairment in iBAT responsiveness to sympathetic activation.
source: This indicates that elevated iBAT thermogenesis in Agrp-IRES-cre mice was not the result of an impairment in iBAT responsiveness to sympathetic activation.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from β-adrenergic stimulation experiment.

claim: iBAT norepinephrine turnover was increased in AGRP-CA-S6 mice compared to control.
source: Instead, increased iBAT norepinephrine turnover in AGRP-CA-S6 mice compared to control indicated increased sympathetic tone to iBAT following constitutive activation of S6K in AGRP neurons (Figure 4i; NETO: −0.75 pM/mg/h vs. −1.26 pM/mg/h in WT-CA-S6 and AGRP-CA-S6 respectively, p<0.05).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4i.

claim: Constitutive activation of S6K in AGRP neurons increased sympathetic tone to iBAT.
source: Instead, increased iBAT norepinephrine turnover in AGRP-CA-S6 mice compared to control indicated increased sympathetic tone to iBAT following constitutive activation of S6K in AGRP neurons (Figure 4i; NETO: −0.75 pM/mg/h vs. −1.26 pM/mg/h in WT-CA-S6 and AGRP-CA-S6 respectively, p<0.05).
evidence: Conclusion drawn from NETO data.

claim: Constitutive activation of S6K1 in AGRP neurons increased iBAT temperature during a fast.
source: Constitutive activation of S6K1 in AGRP neurons also increased iBAT temperature (Figure 4j)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4j.

claim: Constitutive activation of S6K1 in AGRP neurons increased energy expenditure during a fast.
source: Constitutive activation of S6K1 in AGRP neurons also increased iBAT temperature (Figure 4j) energy expenditure (Figure 4k) during a fast
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4k.

claim: Constitutive activation of S6K1 in AGRP neurons resulted in enhanced body weight loss during a fast.
source: Constitutive activation of S6K1 in AGRP neurons also increased iBAT temperature (Figure 4j) energy expenditure (Figure 4k) during a fast resulting in enhanced body weight loss (Figure 4l).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4l.

claim: Postprandial increases in iBAT thermogenesis were higher in mice expressing constitutively active S6K1 in AGRP neurons.
source: Postprandial increases in iBAT thermogenesis and energy expenditure were also higher in mice expressing constitutively active S6K1 in AGRP neurons (Figure 4l and m).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4l and m.

claim: Postprandial increases in energy expenditure were higher in mice expressing constitutively active S6K1 in AGRP neurons.
source: Postprandial increases in iBAT thermogenesis and energy expenditure were also higher in mice expressing constitutively active S6K1 in AGRP neurons (Figure 4l and m).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4l and m.

claim: Constitutive activation of S6K signaling in AGRP neurons of adult normally developed mice protects against diet-induced weight gain through an increase in sympathetic tone to iBAT and an increase in iBAT thermogenesis.
source: Thus, constitutive activation of S6K signaling in AGRP neurons of adult normally developed mice protect against diet-induced weight gain through an increase in sympathetic tone to iBAT and an increase in iBAT thermogenesis.
evidence: Summary conclusion drawn from multiple experimental observations in Agrp-CA-S6 mice.

claim: Over 95% of the cells expressing the pCDH-CMV-FLEX-HA-S6K1-KR construct were Npy-GFP neurons.
source: Ha staining indicated that over 95% of the cells expressing the construct were Npy-GFP neurons and that over 40% of Npy-GFP cells expressed the construct (Figure 5—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1a.

claim: Over 40% of Npy-GFP cells expressed the pCDH-CMV-FLEX-HA-S6K1-KR construct.
source: Ha staining indicated that over 95% of the cells expressing the construct were Npy-GFP neurons and that over 40% of Npy-GFP cells expressed the construct (Figure 5—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1a.

claim: Decreased expression of p-rpS6 in ARH Npy-GFP neurons confirmed inhibition of the pathway in AGRP neurons of Agrp-DN-S6 mice compared to controls.
source: Decreased expression of p-rpS6 in ARH Npy-GFP neurons confirmed inhibition of the pathway in AGRP neurons of Agrp-DN-S6 mice compared to controls (Figure 5—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Quenching endogenous S6K1 in AGRP neurons was not sufficient to affect body weight gain during chow maintenance.
source: Quenching endogenous S6K1 in AGRP neurons produced changes in energy expenditure reciprocal to those observed following constitutive activation of the pathway. These were not sufficient to affect body weight gain during chow maintenance (Figure 5—figure supplement 1c)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1c.

claim: Quenching endogenous S6K1 in AGRP neurons produced a significant decrease in energy expenditure after switch to a HF diet.
source: Quenching endogenous S6K1 in AGRP neurons produced changes in energy expenditure reciprocal to those observed following constitutive activation of the pathway. These were not sufficient to affect body weight gain during chow maintenance (Figure 5—figure supplement 1c) but produced a significant decrease in energy expenditure (Figure 5a)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5a.

claim: Quenching endogenous S6K1 in AGRP neurons produced a significant decrease in locomotor activity after switch to a HF diet.
source: Quenching endogenous S6K1 in AGRP neurons produced changes in energy expenditure reciprocal to those observed following constitutive activation of the pathway. These were not sufficient to affect body weight gain during chow maintenance (Figure 5—figure supplement 1c) but produced a significant decrease in energy expenditure (Figure 5a), locomotor activity (Figure 5b)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5b.

claim: Quenching endogenous S6K1 in AGRP neurons produced a significant decrease in iBAT temperature after switch to a HF diet.
source: Quenching endogenous S6K1 in AGRP neurons produced changes in energy expenditure reciprocal to those observed following constitutive activation of the pathway. These were not sufficient to affect body weight gain during chow maintenance (Figure 5—figure supplement 1c) but produced a significant decrease in energy expenditure (Figure 5a), locomotor activity (Figure 5b), iBAT temperature (Figure 5c)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5c.

claim: Quenching endogenous S6K1 in AGRP neurons produced a significant decrease in iBAT thermogenic gene expression after switch to a HF diet.
source: Quenching endogenous S6K1 in AGRP neurons produced changes in energy expenditure reciprocal to those observed following constitutive activation of the pathway. These were not sufficient to affect body weight gain during chow maintenance (Figure 5—figure supplement 1c) but produced a significant decrease in energy expenditure (Figure 5a), locomotor activity (Figure 5b), iBAT temperature (Figure 5c), and iBAT thermogenic gene expression (Figure 5d) after switch to a HF diet.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5d.

claim: Downregulation of S6K1 activity in AGRP neurons produced a modest reduction in weight gain during the initial switch to HFD.
source: Downregulation of S6K1 activity in AGRP neurons only produced a modest reduction in weight gain during the initial switch to HFD (Figure 5e)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5e.

claim: During the initial switch to HFD, there were no differences in food intake between Agrp-DN-S6 and control mice.
source: Downregulation of S6K1 activity in AGRP neurons only produced a modest reduction in weight gain during the initial switch to HFD (Figure 5e) during which time we did not observe any differences in food intake (Figure 5f)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5f.

claim: During the initial switch to HFD, there were no differences in RER between Agrp-DN-S6 and control mice.
source: Downregulation of S6K1 activity in AGRP neurons only produced a modest reduction in weight gain during the initial switch to HFD (Figure 5e) during which time we did not observe any differences in food intake (Figure 5f) or RER (Figure 5—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1d.

claim: A reduction in food intake was observed in Agrp-DN-S6 mice 4 days after the introduction of the HF diet.
source: However, we observed a reduction in food intake in DN-S6K mice 4 days after the introduction of the HF diet (Figure 5f)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5f.

claim: The reduction in food intake in Agrp-DN-S6 mice likely occurred secondary to reduced energy expenditure and mitigated changes in weight gain.
source: However, we observed a reduction in food intake in DN-S6K mice 4 days after the introduction of the HF diet (Figure 5f), an effect that likely occurred secondary to reduced energy expenditure and mitigated changes in weight gain.
evidence: Interpretation of the temporal relationship between energy expenditure and food intake changes.

claim: Agrp-DN-S6 mice lose significantly less weight than wild-type controls during an overnight fast.
source: Despite showing no difference in body weight under ad libitum access to food, Agrp-DN-S6 mice lose significantly less weight than wild-type controls during an overnight fast (Figure 5g)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5g.

claim: Agrp-DN-S6 mice show increased energy efficiency during an overnight fast.
source: Despite showing no difference in body weight under ad libitum access to food, Agrp-DN-S6 mice lose significantly less weight than wild-type controls during an overnight fast (Figure 5g), indicating increased energy efficiency in these mice.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from reduced weight loss during fasting.

claim: Energy expenditure was lower in Agrp-DN-S6 mice throughout the fast.
source: Consistently, energy expenditure was lower in Agrp-DN-S6 mice throughout the fast (Figure 5h).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5h.

claim: Postprandial increases in energy expenditure during refeed was lower in Agrp-DN-S6 mice.
source: In addition, postprandial increases in energy expenditure (Figure 5h) during the subsequent refeed was lower.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5h.

claim: Body weight gain at thermoneutrality was significantly higher in Agrp-DN-S6 mice than in controls.
source: Last, body weight gain at thermoneutrality was significantly higher in Agrp-DN-S6 mice than in controls (Figure 5i).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5i.

claim: Downregulation of S6K signaling in AGRP neurons leads to a decrease in energy expenditure mediated at least in part by a decrease in iBAT thermogenesis, which leads to a significant increase in body weight gain when mice are maintained at thermoneutrality.
source: Collectively, these data indicate that downregulation of S6K signaling in AGRP neurons leads to a decrease in energy expenditure mediated at least in part by a decrease in iBAT thermogenesis, which leads to a significant increase in body weight gain when mice are maintained at thermoneutrality.
evidence: Summary conclusion drawn from multiple experimental observations in Agrp-DN-S6 mice.

claim: Central leptin engages the sympathetic nervous system to increase iBAT thermogenesis through the activation of distributed leptin-receptor expressing neurons in the DMH, nMPO, NTS and ARH.
source: Central leptin engages the sympathetic nervous system to increase iBAT thermogenesis through the activation of distributed leptin-receptor expressing neurons in the DMH, nMPO, NTS and ARH.
evidence: Statement of established knowledge in the field.

claim: Leptin receptors in the ARH play a role in leptin-induced activation of iBAT.
source: Several lines of evidence support a role for leptin receptors in the ARH in leptin-induced activation of iBAT (Rahmouni and Morgan, 2007; Harlan et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Rahmouni and Morgan, 2007 and Harlan et al., 2011.

claim: In the adult brain, leptin inhibits the vast majority of AGRP neurons.
source: In the adult brain, leptin inhibits the vast majority of AGRP neurons (Baquero et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Baquero et al., 2014.

claim: Previous work implicated hypothalamic mTORC1 signaling in leptin's effects on energy balance.
source: Previous work implicated hypothalamic mTORC1 signaling in leptin's effects on energy balance (Cota et al., 2006; Blouet et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cota et al., 2006 and Blouet et al., 2008.

claim: Leptin increased the expression of p-mTOR in NPY/AGRP neurons 30 min following leptin administration.
source: Leptin increased the expression of p-mTOR (Figure 6a and c)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6a and c.

claim: Leptin increased the expression of the active form of ribosomal protein S6 (p-rpS6) in NPY/AGRP neurons 30 min following leptin administration.
source: Leptin increased the expression of p-mTOR (Figure 6a and c) and the expression of the active form of one of its effectors, ribosomal protein S6 (p-rpS6, Figure 6b and d) in NPY/AGRP neurons.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6b and d.

claim: Leptin increased expression of pSTAT3 in NPY/AGRP neurons.
source: As expected, leptin increased expression of pSTAT3 in NPY/AGRP neurons
evidence: Supported by experimental observation.

claim: 40% of pSTAT-3+ NPY/AGRP neurons also expressed the active form of rpS6.
source: As expected, leptin increased expression of pSTAT3 in NPY/AGRP neurons, and we observed that 40% of pSTAT-3+ NPY/AGRP neurons also expressed the active form of rpS6.
evidence: Supported by quantification of immunofluorescence data.

claim: Leptin's effects on temperature were attenuated in Agrp-CA-S6 mice compared to wild-type controls.
source: Leptin's effects on temperature were attenuated in Agrp-CA-S6 mice compared to wild-type controls (Figure 6e).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6e.

claim: Lack of flexibility in mTORC1 signaling in AGRP neurons impairs leptin's thermogenic action.
source: While both groups reached a similar absolute temperature increase following ip leptin, the relative change in temperature was significantly lower in the Agrp-CA-S6 mice due to their elevated core temperature at baseline. Together these data suggest that lack of flexibility in mTORC1 signaling in AGRP neurons impairs leptin's thermogenic action.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from leptin challenge in Agrp-CA-S6 mice.

claim: Leptin's thermogenic effect was completely abolished in Agrp-DN-S6 mice.
source: Leptin's thermogenic effect was completely abolished in Agrp-DN-S6 mice (Figure 6f)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6f.

claim: S6K1 signaling in AGRP neurons is required for leptin's thermogenic action.
source: Leptin's thermogenic effect was completely abolished in Agrp-DN-S6 mice (Figure 6f), indicating that S6K1 signaling in AGRP neurons is required for leptin's thermogenic action.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the abolishment of leptin's effect in Agrp-DN-S6 mice.

claim: Activation of AGRP neurons induces a rapid suppression of sympathetic output to iBAT, leading to a decrease in iBAT thermogenesis and energy expenditure.
source: Here, we demonstrate that the multimodal contribution of AGRP neurons to the maintenance of energy balance includes the regulation of iBAT thermogenesis. We show that activation of AGRP neurons induces a rapid suppression of sympathetic output to iBAT, as previously reported (Steculorum et al., 2016), leading to a decrease in iBAT thermogenesis and energy expenditure.
evidence: Summary statement with citation to Steculorum et al., 2016.

claim: The AGRP-iBAT circuit is selectively engaged to spare internal energy stores in the absence of food and food sensory cues.
source: We show that the AGRP-iBAT circuit is selectively engaged to spare internal energy stores in the absence of food and food sensory cues
evidence: Summary conclusion from experiments with different food availability conditions.

claim: AGRP neurons integrate external and internal signals of energy availability to coordinate energy intake and expenditure in conditions of low energy availability.
source: We show that the AGRP-iBAT circuit is selectively engaged to spare internal energy stores in the absence of food and food sensory cues, supporting the notion that AGRP neurons integrate external and internal signals of energy availability to coordinate energy intake and expenditure in conditions of low energy availability.
evidence: Summary conclusion from multiple experimental observations.

claim: The mTORC1 signaling pathway is an intracellular mechanism through which AGRP neurons monitor external and internal energy availability.
source: We provide evidence that this regulation also occurs at thermoneutrality and is therefore potentially relevant to human physiology. We identify the mTORC1 signaling pathway as an intracellular mechanism through which AGRP neurons monitor external and internal energy availability
evidence: Summary conclusion from mTORC1 manipulation experiments.

claim: mTORC1 signaling modulates AGRP activity, sympathetic tone to iBAT, iBAT thermogenesis and energy expenditure.
source: We identify the mTORC1 signaling pathway as an intracellular mechanism through which AGRP neurons monitor external and internal energy availability, and demonstrate that mTORC1 signaling modulates AGRP activity, sympathetic tone to iBAT, iBAT thermogenesis and energy expenditure.
evidence: Summary conclusion from mTORC1 manipulation experiments.

claim: Metabolic sensing via mTORC1 in AGRP neurons is required for the regulation of energy expenditure both during nutritional transitions from fasting to feeding and during adaptation to HF feeding.
source: Last, we show that metabolic sensing via mTORC1 in AGRP neurons is required for the regulation of energy expenditure both during nutritional transitions from fasting to feeding and during adaptation to HF feeding.
evidence: Summary conclusion from experiments in different nutritional contexts.
